content: 1. Facilities that provide maternity and newborn services must have a clearly documented breastfeeding policy. This policy should be routinely communicated to all staff and parents. Although this recommendation is based on very low-quality evidence, it is strongly advised. 2. Healthcare staff involved in infant feeding services, including breastfeeding support, must possess adequate knowledge, skills, and competence to effectively assist women in breastfeeding. This recommendation is also based on very low-quality evidence but remains essential. 3. Pregnant women and their families should receive counseling on the benefits and management of breastfeeding during antenatal care. This recommendation is supported by moderate-quality evidence. 4. Discharge planning from maternity and newborn facilities should ensure that parents and their infants have access to ongoing breastfeeding support and appropriate care. This coordination is vital for protecting, promoting, and supporting breastfeeding. The evidence supporting this recommendation is of low quality. 5. Immediate and focused support to initiate and establish breastfeeding within the first hours and days of life has long-term positive effects beyond the hospital stay. 6. Evidence supports the benefits of immediate and uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact starting within 10 minutes of delivery. However, this practice can often begin even earlier, within 2–3 minutes after delivery, while necessary assessments, drying, and suctioning (if needed) are performed during skin-to-skin contact. 7. Uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact should ideally last for more than an hour. Longer durations should be encouraged if well-tolerated by both mother and infant. 8. During early skin-to-skin contact and for at least the first two hours after delivery, healthcare personnel should maintain vigilant observation to assess and manage any signs of distress in the mother or infant. 9. Early initiation of breastfeeding within the first hour after delivery has been shown to have significant positive effects. Among healthy term infants, feeding cues may appear within the first 15–20 minutes after birth or later. 10. There is a dose-response effect in breastfeeding initiation, meaning earlier initiation results in greater benefits. Mothers unable to initiate breastfeeding within the first hour, such as those undergoing cesarean delivery or experiencing medical instability, should still be supported to breastfeed as soon as they are able. 11. Mothers should be supported to achieve effective breastfeeding, including proper positioning and attachment of the infant to the breast, responding to feeding cues, and expressing breast milk when necessary. 12. Expressing breast milk is a valuable technique not only for separated mothers and infants but also for stimulating attachment and effective sucking during the establishment of breastfeeding. 13. Mothers of infants admitted to neonatal intensive care units should be sensitively supported to enable skin-to-skin contact, recognize their infants’ behavioral cues, and effectively express breast milk soon after birth. 14. Additional foods and fluids apart from breast milk should only be given when medically justified. Lack of resources, staff time, or knowledge is not a valid reason for early supplementation. 15. Proper guidance and counseling for mothers and family members are essential to help them make informed decisions about the use or avoidance of pacifiers, feeding bottles, and teats until breastfeeding is successfully established. 16. Supporting mothers to respond to their infants’ behavioral cues for feeding, comfort, or closeness fosters nurturing relationships, builds maternal confidence, and enhances breastfeeding success and infant development. Responses may include breastfeeding, skin-to-skin contact, cuddling, carrying, talking, or singing. 17. There should be no promotion of breast-milk substitutes, feeding bottles, teats, pacifiers, or dummies in maternity and newborn facilities or by their staff. 18. Health facilities and staff must not provide feeding bottles, teats, or other products covered by the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes and related WHA resolutions to breastfeeding infants. 19. Creating an enabling environment for breastfeeding includes having policies and guidelines that uphold quality standards for promoting, protecting, and supporting breastfeeding in maternity and newborn facilities. These policies should align with the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes and related WHA resolutions. 20. Relevant training for healthcare workers is essential to ensure the effective implementation of quality standards according to their roles. 21. Parents should be offered antenatal breastfeeding education tailored to their individual needs, delivered sensitively, and considering their social and cultural context. This preparation helps them address potential challenges. 22. Mothers should be prepared for discharge by ensuring they can feed and care for their infants and have access to continued breastfeeding support. Post-discharge support in the following days and weeks is crucial for addressing early breastfeeding challenges. 23. Minimizing disruptions to breastfeeding during the hospital stay requires healthcare practices that allow mothers to breastfeed as much, as frequently, and for as long as they wish. 24. Coordination of clinical systems in maternity and newborn facilities, ensuring consistent breastfeeding support across obstetric, midwifery, and pediatric services, improves outcomes for mothers and infants. 25. Research gaps exist in areas such as the impact of breastfeeding education and training for healthcare workers, family involvement in breastfeeding education, and the effects of skin-to-skin contact among less healthy or unstable parent-infant pairs. Further research is needed to address these gaps and improve breastfeeding outcomes. 26. The WHO will continue to monitor research developments in breastfeeding protection, promotion, and support, particularly for recommendations with low or very low-quality evidence. Updates to the guidelines will follow formal WHO procedures as new evidence becomes available.
